# How to fix "Uncaught ReflectionException: Class view does not exist" in Laravel after deployment to Ubuntu 18.04 server

When migrating a Laravel application from an older environment like Ubuntu 16.04 to a fresh installation of Ubuntu 18.04, you might encounter a baffling error that seems unrelated to the OS upgrade itself. The stack trace often points directly to `Illuminate/Container/Container.php:788`:

```php
$reflector = new ReflectionClass($concrete);
```

And the message reads: `Uncaught ReflectionException: Class view does not exist`. At first glance, this suggests that Laravel cannot find the `view` class, which is a core component of the framework. However, since you have already cleared the config cache and run `composer dump-autoload` without success, the root cause usually lies in how Composer resolves dependencies during the fresh install.

The error occurs because the container tries to resolve an alias or abstract that isn't properly bound in the current environment. In many cases, this happens when a package vendor directory is missing or incomplete on the new server. Specifically, if you are using packages like `laravel/ui` or any custom artisan commands that rely on specific view composers or extensions, Composer might not have fully populated the necessary autoloader maps for those classes on the Ubuntu 18.04 machine.

To resolve this, you must ensure that all vendor dependencies are correctly installed and that the autoload files are regenerated. Start by navigating to your project root and running:

```bash
composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader
```

The `--optimize-autoloader` flag is critical here. It generates a single static map file that maps every class to its location, which can significantly speed up autoload resolution and prevent missing class errors during deployment. If you are using PHP 7.3 or higher (which Ubuntu 18.04 supports natively), this optimization step is even more important for performance and stability.

If the issue persists after regenerating the autoloader, inspect your `composer.json` file to ensure that there are no conflicting version constraints that might cause Composer to skip downloading certain packages silently. Sometimes, a dependency conflict can lead to incomplete installation where core classes like `Illuminate\View\Factory` are not fully available in the namespace hierarchy.

Another common pitfall during migration is the difference in PHP versions between the two servers. While Ubuntu 16.04 often came with older PHP builds (like 7.0 or 7.1) and Ubuntu 18.04 offers newer ones (7.3+), some older Laravel versions may not be fully compatible with the latest PHP features unless you have run `composer update` to align your dependencies with the new runtime environment.

Ensure that your `composer.lock` file is either committed to version control or regenerated on the new server using:

```bash
composer update --lock
```

This ensures that the lock file matches the actual installed packages, preventing subtle mismatches where a class exists in the source but not in the vendor directory due to locked versions.

Finally, if you are still seeing the error, check your `app/Providers/AppServiceProvider.php` or any custom service provider for bindings that might reference non-existent classes. Sometimes, when moving to a new environment, configuration paths change, and hardcoded class names in providers can break. Reviewing these files ensures that no stale references remain after the migration.

For further assistance with Laravel deployment challenges or compatibility issues across different operating systems, you can refer to [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com).
